'''''Cosmos atrosanguineus''''', the '''chocolate cosmos''', is a species of ''[[Cosmos (plant)|Cosmos]]'', native to [[Mexico]]. It has often been claimed that it is [[extinct in the wild]]; however it is truly abundant in Mexico. The species was introduced into cultivation in 1885, when the British seed company Thompson & Morgan first listed it in their seed catalogue.<ref name=Rice17/> Its dark red to brownish red flowers have a scent resembling chocolate, which is one reason for its popularity as a cultivated plant.

==Description==
''Cosmos atrosanguineus'' is a [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] growing to 40–60 cm tall, with a fleshy [[tuber]]ous root. The [[leaf|leaves]] are 7–15 cm long, [[pinnate]], with leaflets 2–5 cm long. The [[flower]]s are produced in a [[inflorescence|capitulum]] 3–4.5 cm diameter, dark red to maroon-dark brown, with a ring of six to ten (usually eight) broad [[ray florets]] and a center of [[disc floret]]s; they have a light [[vanillin]] fragrance (like many [[chocolate]]s), which becomes more noticeable towards the end of the day.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sfgate.com/homeandgarden/article/Plants-that-make-the-mouth-water-3170426.php|title=Plants that make the mouth water|date=22 February 2009}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The species was first described in 1861 by [[William Jackson Hooker|William Hooker]], as ''Cosmos diversifolia'' var. ''atrosanguineus''. [[Eduard Ortgies]] later elevated it to a full species, placing it in the genus ''[[Bidens]]''. [[Andreas Voss (botanist)|Andreas Voss]] transferred it back to ''Cosmos'', retaining its status as an independent species. It is one of eight species of ''Cosmos'' placed in section ''Discopoda''. ''Cosmos'' belongs to subtribe Coreopsidinae.<ref name=Rice17/>

In 2008, Oku, T.; Takahashi, H.; Yagi, F.; et al. analyzed the Chocolate Cosmos flower using PSID (plastid subtype identity) sequences in order to clarify the phylogenetic relationships of this plant. They determined that this species did indeed have closer relations to ''Cosmos'' than to the genus of ''Bidens'' or ''Dahlia.''

==Distribution and habitat==
Although it had been reported that ''Cosmos atrosanguineus'' was [[extinct in the wild]], a research project on the genus ''[[Cosmos (plant)|Cosmos]]'' begun in 2007 by Mexican botanist Aarón Rodríguez found modern records starting from 1986. Field work showed that it grew in the states of [[Guanajuato]], [[Querétaro]] and [[San Luis Potosí]]. It is found in mixed pine and oak forest, at elevations of around {{cvt|1800|–|2450|m|ft}}.<ref name=Rice17/>

==Cultivation and uses==
Both seed-raised and vegetatively propagated [[cultivar]]s are available, varying in the size, colour and shape of the petals. An article in 2017 listed 17 cultivars and seed-raised strains. {{As of|2018}}, ''C.'' ''atrosanguineus'' 'Hamcoec' (trade description {{tdes|Eclipse}}) has the largest flower heads, up to 5 cm in diameter.<ref name=Rice17/> The variation in flower color from red to black of ''Cosmos atrosanguineus'' and its cultivars results from variation in the amounts of [[anthocyanin]]s and [[chalcone]] present.<ref>Amamiya, K., & Iwashina, T. (2016). [http://europepmc.org/abstract/med/26996024 "Qualitative and Quantitative Analysis of Flower Pigments in Chocolate Cosmos, Cosmos atrosanguineus, and its Hybrids"]. ''Natural Product Communications'', 11(1), 77–78.</ref> Hybrids with other ''Cosmos'' species are also known in cultivation. As with ''Cosmos'' 'Thomocha' ({{tdes|Chocamocha}}), hybrids may be less scented than the species.<ref name=Rice17/> Although cosmos smells like chocolate, it should not be eaten.<ref name="flower flood">{{cite web |last1=kenan |first1=kenanist28 |title=Exotic Flowers That Will Leave You in Awe |url=https://flowerflood.com/cosmos-flower-meaning-and-symbolism/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230530062956/https://flowerflood.com/cosmos-flower-meaning-and-symbolism/ |archive-date=May 30, 2023 |access-date=30 May 2023 |website=flower flood}}</ref>

It requires partial sun or full sun, and flowers from mid to late summer. It is frost-sensitive (Zones 6–11); in temperate zones, the tuber has to be dug up and stored in a frost-free store over the winter.
